source_read: PMC HTML, PMC2413312: abstract, all sections (introduction, therapeutic uses, pharmacologic actions, dopamine and craving, brain damage, treatment), Figure 1-2 legends, acknowledgments, competing interests; reference list checked for refs 1, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 18, 20, 28-30. Short narrative review (CMAJ, 4 pages), no tables.

claims.overstatement: 'So a single dose remains pharmacologically active for most of a day' is not in this source and is an inference from half-life alone: plasma presence is not the same as activity (in Hart 2008, subjective effects returned toward baseline within about 4 h while plasma was at its peak; cardiovascular effects lasted beyond 4 h). Suggest 'remains in the blood for most of a day' or cite effect-duration data.
claims.note: Kish gives about 11 h for smoked, intranasal and intravenous routes, but second-hand: it is cited to ref 1 (Schifano et al., a review of smokable amphetamine-type stimulants), not to a primary pharmacokinetic study; it gives no range. Onset: oral therapeutic forms 'slow-onset (e.g., 20-60 minutes)' vs smokable forms 'seconds to minutes' (refs 8, 9; ref 9 is the Erowid website); intravenous is described only as having comparably high bioavailability, so 'fastest after ... injection' is not stated here, though uncontroversial. The lower end '10' of '10-11 hours' must come from another source.

anchors.extracted: Elimination half-life of smoked crystal methamphetamine and of methamphetamine taken intranasally or intravenously about 11 h (cited to ref 1, Schifano et al. review). Smoked form gives a very rapid and intense high; intravenous form has comparably high bioavailability.

anchors.locator: Therapeutic uses of methamphetamine and amphetamine, para 2
anchors.extracted: Contrasts slow-onset oral therapeutic forms (about 20-60 min) with very fast-onset smokable forms (seconds to minutes; refs 8, 9).

claims.note: Kish's 2008 position matches the claim's 'not established': low striatal dopamine in some users' brains, uncertain whether neuronal loss; modestly decreased striatal DAT in some recreational users, with whether this is terminal loss 'debated'. It also leans the other way in one sentence: from animal data it is 'reasonable to expect' that terminal damage would occur in people at some dose. The Parkinson's-pattern part of the claim is not discussed here except via the cited autopsy paper's title (ref 20, 'Why is parkinsonism not a feature of human methamphetamine users?').

anchors.locator: Abstract; Does methamphetamine cause brain damage?, paras 1-2
anchors.extracted: Imaging findings too preliminary to define a characteristic pattern; high-dose methamphetamine damages striatal dopamine terminals in animals and the author considers it reasonable to expect similar damage in people at some dose; no evidence of terminal damage at therapeutic amphetamine doses; some recreational users show modestly lower striatal DAT, and whether this is loss of terminals or clinically relevant is debated. Abstract: low dopamine in some users' brains, but whether this means neuronal loss is uncertain.

anchors.locator: Is there a role for dopamine in methamphetamine-craving?, para 1
anchors.extracted: Autopsy: low striatal dopamine in recreational users (ref 20), interpreted as depletion by the amounts used.

claims.note: Qualifies the laboratory claim in two ways: it lists the same acute effects (alertness, energy, well-being, euphoria at high doses, appetite suppression, raised heart rate and blood pressure, fatal at high doses), and it shows that real-world exposure can far exceed laboratory exposure: a single 30 mg smoked dose gave peak plasma about 50 ng/ml, while blood levels in unsupervised recreational users in a police investigation ranged 15-1,600 ng/ml (median 190), and binge use raises levels further. Laboratory single doses therefore sample only the lower part of real-world exposure.

anchors.locator: Therapeutic uses..., para 3; Pharmacologic actions of methamphetamine, para 1
anchors.extracted: A single smoked 30 mg dose: peak plasma about 50 ng/ml (ref 8); 'real-life' blood levels in unsupervised users 15-1,600 ng/ml, median 190 (ref 12, Melega et al. 2007); repeated (binge) dosing gives much higher levels; typical acute effects: alertness, wakefulness, energy, well-being, euphoria at high doses, appetite suppression, increased heart rate and blood pressure, death possible at high doses.

claims.note: Qualifies only: real-world and binge exposure exceeds what laboratory single-dose studies tested, which supports the claim's closing caveat ('repeated or binge use was not tested'). Kish does not address acute cognitive effects of single doses; it mentions low dopamine possibly explaining aspects of cognitive impairment during withdrawal.

anchors.locator: Therapeutic uses..., para 3; Is there a role for dopamine..., para 1
anchors.extracted: Binge use produces much higher drug levels than single doses; real-world blood levels median 190 ng/ml (range 15-1,600); low striatal dopamine might explain aspects of cognitive impairment and withdrawal dysphoria.

reporting_issues.note: Ref 18 is Heimer 2003, Am J Psychiatry (anatomical framework).
Ref 20 is Moszczynska et al. 2004, Brain (post-mortem).

missed: Key finding 3 (half-life about 11 h) is itself second-hand: the sentence cites ref 1, Schifano et al., a review of smokable amphetamine-type stimulants, and gives no range or primary pharmacokinetic study. cl_meth_pk_halflife currently cites Kish 2008 for the 11 h figure; a primary PK source should be anchored, as the claim's magnitude field already anticipates.
Kish does not support the claim's inference that a single dose 'remains pharmacologically active for most of a day'; it gives only the half-life.

Therapeutic uses section, para 2 (onset): oral therapeutic forms 'slow-onset (e.g., 20-60 minutes)' vs smokable forms 'seconds to minutes' - the anchor for the onset part of cl_meth_pk_halflife; not among the card's key findings.
